Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Of course the TV series Miami Vice seems dated now, but it's not just because Don Johnson's white Armani suits and slip-on shoes belong to a mercifully bygone era. The fact is, Miami is no longer the same city as the one portrayed in the 1980s cop show. Party time in Little Havana. The expansive sandy beaches are still there, as is the surfeit of sunshine, the hint of the exotic and the hordes of sun-hungry tourists who have flocked to this holiday hotspot for the last 80 years. But Miami has shed much of its unwanted baggage from the 80s and has grown beyond a resort town into something more substantial. Still barely 100 years old, Miami was a tourist destination almost from its inception. The offshore sandbar called Miami Beach was quickly recognized as having all the ingredients of a world-class holiday resort and the hotel-building spree that took place in the 1920s and 30s has left Miami Beach with hundreds of stunning Art Deco structures that give the area its distinctive look . By the 1980s, as well as being the destination of choice for holiday makers, retirees and 'snowbirds' (Canadians and northern Americans wintering in Florida), Miami had attracted an uninvited guest -- the 'cocaine cowboy.' Miami's proximity to South America made it a key point of entry for Colombian cocaine smugglers and the city became a battleground for ruthless drug barons intent on grabbing their piece of the American Dream. The mid 80s was the Miami Vice era, when the city's reputation for glamour and hedonism came with a side order of carjackings and gangland shootouts. But by the mid 90s, Miami had largely driven the cocaine cowboys out of town and hoteliers like Ian Schrager began converting some of those Art Deco classics into sophisticated boutique hotels fit for the international jet set. The guns may have gone but the glitz was never far away. Now that Miami's been to rehab and come out cleaned up and healthy, it turns out there's more to the city than glitzy nightclubs and the surgically enhanced bodies of the beautiful people. Miami has acquired a reputation as the new kid on the block in the modern art scene, a reputation that was cemented when the world's most prestigious modern art fair, Art Basel, arrived in the city in 2002. Just like the snowbirds, Art Basel returns to Miami each winter and the Wynwood neighborhood has now become a bona fide art district, with exclusive galleries showcasing cutting-edge art all year round. Nearby, the Design District is full of studios and workshops producing contemporary furniture and art. Then there's the fact that Miami is one of the most cosmopolitan cities in the world, with some 60% of the population born outside the U.S. The food, music, culture and language of Latin America have all become part of modern Miami, giving the city a cultural heritage that belies its youth. But don't think Miami's reinvention as a cultural destination has done anything to dent it's appetite for the good times. When it comes to partying, there's not many places that can keep up with Miami, and even fewer that can do it with as much style. In truth, there's still a touch of the old Vice about Miami, and who knows, with the 80s revival, we may not have seen the last of those white suits.

(CNN) — Of course, the TV series *Miami Vice* seems dated now, but not simply because Don Johnson’s white Armani suits and slip-on shoes belong to a mercifully bygone era. The fact is that Miami is no longer the city portrayed in the 1980s cop show.

Party time in Little Havana.

The expansive sandy beaches remain, along with the abundant sunshine, a hint of the exotic, and the hordes of sun-seeking tourists who have flocked to this holiday hotspot for the past 80 years. But Miami has shed much of its unwanted baggage from the 1980s and evolved beyond a resort town into something more substantial.

Still barely 100 years old, Miami was a tourist destination almost from its inception. The offshore sandbar known as Miami Beach was quickly recognized as having all the ingredients of a world-class holiday resort. The hotel-building boom of the 1920s and 1930s left Miami Beach with hundreds of stunning Art Deco structures that give the area its distinctive character.

By the 1980s, in addition to being the destination of choice for holidaymakers, retirees, and “snowbirds” — Canadians and northern Americans spending the winter in Florida — Miami had attracted an uninvited guest: the “cocaine cowboy.”

Miami’s proximity to South America made it a key entry point for Colombian cocaine smugglers, and the city became a battleground for ruthless drug barons intent on claiming their piece of the American Dream. The mid-1980s marked the *Miami Vice* era, when the city’s reputation for glamour and hedonism came with a side order of carjackings and gangland shootouts.

By the mid-1990s, however, Miami had largely driven the cocaine cowboys out of town, and hoteliers such as Ian Schrager began transforming some of those Art Deco classics into sophisticated boutique hotels fit for the international jet set. The guns may have disappeared, but the glitz was never far away.

Now that Miami has been to rehab and emerged cleaner and healthier, it turns out there is more to the city than glittering nightclubs and the surgically enhanced bodies of the beautiful people.

Miami has earned a reputation as the new kid on the block in the modern art world — a status cemented in 2002, when Art Basel, the world’s most prestigious modern art fair, arrived in the city. Like the snowbirds, Art Basel returns to Miami each winter, while the Wynwood neighborhood has become a bona fide arts district, with exclusive galleries showcasing cutting-edge work year-round. Nearby, the Design District is filled with studios and workshops producing contemporary furniture and art.

Miami is also one of the world’s most cosmopolitan cities, with some 60% of its population born outside the United States. The food, music, culture, and languages of Latin America have all become part of modern Miami, giving the city a cultural heritage that belies its youth.

But do not imagine that Miami’s reinvention as a cultural destination has diminished its appetite for a good time. When it comes to partying, few places can keep pace with Miami, and even fewer can do so with such style.

In truth, there is still a touch of the old *Vice* about Miami. And with the 1980s revival, who knows? We may not have seen the last of those white suits.

(CNN) — *Miami Vice* inevitably looks like a product of another age, and not only because Don Johnson’s white Armani outfits and loafers are reminders of a fashion era many are happy to have left behind. Miami itself has changed dramatically since the city depicted in the 1980s police drama.

Little Havana still knows how to celebrate. Miami also retains its broad stretches of sand, abundant sunshine, exotic atmosphere and crowds of sun-seeking visitors, who have been coming to this vacation destination for eight decades. Yet the city has discarded much of the troubling legacy of the 1980s, evolving from a simple beach resort into a place with greater depth and significance.

Although Miami is only a little more than a century old, tourism shaped it almost from the beginning. Developers quickly realized that the offshore sandbar known as Miami Beach had everything needed to become an internationally renowned resort. A hotel construction boom during the 1920s and 1930s produced hundreds of striking Art Deco buildings, which continue to define the neighborhood’s visual character.

By the 1980s, Miami was already popular with vacationers, retirees and “snowbirds”—Canadians and residents of the northern United States who spent their winters in Florida. But it had also become home to a far less welcome figure: the “cocaine cowboy.”

Because of Miami’s closeness to South America, the city became an important gateway for Colombian cocaine traffickers. Violent drug lords competing for their share of the American Dream turned it into a war zone. In the middle of the decade, at the height of the *Miami Vice* period, Miami’s image combined luxury and pleasure-seeking with carjackings and gun battles between criminal gangs.

By the mid-1990s, however, the city had largely forced the cocaine cowboys out. Hotel entrepreneurs such as Ian Schrager started transforming historic Art Deco properties into stylish boutique accommodations designed for wealthy international travelers. The gunfire had faded, but Miami’s love of glamour remained.

After cleaning up its act and emerging in better shape, Miami revealed that it offered much more than flashy clubs and surgically perfected members of the beautiful set. It began establishing itself as an important newcomer in contemporary art, a status strengthened in 2002 when Art Basel—the world’s most prestigious modern-art fair—came to the city.

Like the winter visitors from the north, Art Basel returns every year. Meanwhile, Wynwood has developed into a genuine arts district, where high-end galleries display innovative work throughout the year. Close by, the Design District is packed with workshops and studios devoted to contemporary art and furniture.

Miami is also among the world’s most internationally diverse cities, with roughly 60 percent of its residents born outside the United States. Latin American cuisine, music, traditions and languages are now deeply woven into the city’s identity, giving this relatively young place a cultural richness that suggests a much longer history.

Still, Miami’s transformation into a cultural destination has not weakened its enthusiasm for having fun. Few cities can rival its nightlife, and fewer still can match the style with which Miami celebrates.

In reality, traces of the old *Vice* remain. And with 1980s fashion making a comeback, those famous white suits may yet return.

Miami has evolved far beyond the glamorous yet crime-ridden city portrayed in the 1980s television series *Miami Vice*. Although beaches, sunshine, and nightlife remain central to its identity, the city has undergone a major social, cultural, and economic transformation.

Miami Beach was originally developed as a tourist destination, and its architectural heritage still reflects that history. During the hotel boom of the 1920s and 1930s, hundreds of distinctive Art Deco buildings were constructed. Many of these structures have survived, giving the area its recognizable style and preserving an important link to its past.

In the 1980s, however, Miami became notorious for drug trafficking and violent crime. Its proximity to South America made it a major entry point for Colombian cocaine. The enormous profits generated by the drug trade fueled gangland conflicts, carjackings, and widespread violence, creating the dangerous image later dramatized in popular culture.

By the mid-1990s, Miami had largely driven out the so-called “cocaine cowboys.” At the same time, developers began restoring historic hotels and transforming them into sophisticated boutique properties designed for international visitors. This revival helped preserve Miami Beach’s architectural character while strengthening the city’s appeal as an upscale global destination.

Today, Miami still offers the tourism, glamour, warm weather, and beaches for which it has long been famous. Yet it has also become cleaner, safer, and more substantial—a diverse, internationally connected city whose identity extends well beyond the stereotypes of its past.
outputs.L4:
Miami has reinvented itself many times. In the early twentieth century, it became famous as a tropical resort, attracting visitors with its warm climate, palm-lined beaches, and distinctive Art Deco hotels. Along Miami Beach, pastel-colored buildings, neon signs, and streamlined façades helped create an image of elegance and escape. The city came to represent sunshine, leisure, and glamour, a place where tourists could enjoy an exotic atmosphere without leaving the United States.

That image changed dramatically in the 1980s. Miami became a major entry point for the cocaine trade, and the vast profits generated by trafficking contributed to corruption, organized crime, and a wave of highly visible violence. Shootings and drug-related murders gave the city a dangerous reputation, while films and television programs presented it as a glamorous but lawless frontier. Luxury cars, fashionable nightclubs, and waterfront mansions existed alongside poverty, social tension, and fear. For many people outside Florida, Miami became almost inseparable from the excesses and violence of the cocaine era.

By the 1990s, however, the city was undergoing another transformation. Falling crime rates, urban redevelopment, and new investment helped restore confidence in Miami. Historic Art Deco buildings were renovated rather than demolished, public spaces were improved, and once-neglected districts began attracting businesses, residents, artists, and visitors. The city also became cleaner and more orderly, gradually weakening the image of Miami as a place defined by drugs and danger.

The revival did not mean abandoning the glamour that had always been central to Miami’s appeal. Instead, the city modernized and refined it. Hotels, restaurants, galleries, and cultural institutions offered a more sophisticated version of the Miami experience. South Beach remained a center of fashion and nightlife, but it also became known for architecture, design, and international culture. At the same time, neighborhoods beyond the beach revealed the city’s broader character, shaped by strong Cuban, Caribbean, Latin American, and other immigrant communities.

Modern Miami therefore presents a more complex identity than either the carefree resort of the Art Deco era or the violent drug capital portrayed in the media during the 1980s. Tourism and nightlife remain important, but they no longer tell the whole story. Miami has developed into an international center of business, art, food, architecture, and culture, with close connections to Latin America and the Caribbean.

The city has not completely escaped problems such as inequality, development pressures, and the lingering influence of its old reputation. Nevertheless, its transformation is striking. Miami has preserved its visual drama, energy, and sense of glamour while becoming cleaner, safer, and more self-assured. Its revival shows how a city once associated with excess and crime can reshape its image without losing the distinctive qualities that made it famous.

counterfactuals.output:
# Beyond “Miami Vice”: How Miami Became a Global Capital of Art, Food and Nightlife

*Once defined in the popular imagination by pastel suits, speedboats and cocaine-fueled excess, Miami has transformed itself into one of America’s most dynamic cultural destinations.*

**Miami, Florida** — At sunset, the city still looks like a scene designed for television.

Neon glows against the facades of South Beach’s Art Deco hotels. Sports cars cruise Ocean Drive. Yachts drift across Biscayne Bay, and music spills from rooftop bars into the warm night air.

For many outsiders, this is the Miami immortalized by the 1980s television series “Miami Vice”: glamorous, dangerous and drenched in tropical color. The show’s fictional detectives chased drug traffickers through a city that reflected a very real era of cocaine wealth, gang violence and rapid change.

But modern Miami has moved far beyond that image.

Today, the city is a multilingual, multicultural crossroads where Latin American, Caribbean, European and American influences collide. It has become a major destination for contemporary art and design, an increasingly ambitious food city and a nightlife capital that no longer fits neatly into the velvet-rope stereotypes of South Beach.

Miami hasn’t erased its past. It has remixed it.

## From cocaine capital to cultural gateway

The “cocaine cowboy” years left a complicated legacy. Drug money and violence shook South Florida in the late 1970s and 1980s, while waves of immigration reshaped the city’s population, politics and identity.

“Miami Vice,” which debuted in 1984, exported a stylized version of that turbulence around the world. Its linen suits, synth-heavy soundtrack and pink-and-turquoise palette became inseparable from Miami itself.

Yet even then, the city was more complex than its television persona.

Cuban exiles had already transformed neighborhoods, businesses and civic life. New arrivals from Haiti, Colombia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America and the Caribbean added languages, traditions and cuisines. Over time, Miami evolved from a seasonal resort town into a global gateway — one that often feels culturally closer to Havana, Bogotá or Caracas than to other American cities.

That international character now powers much of its appeal.

In Brickell, glass towers rise above restaurants and cocktail lounges packed late into the evening. Spanish is spoken as commonly as English. Investors, artists, chefs and entrepreneurs move between Miami and cities across the Americas, helping create a place that is less a conventional US metropolis than a capital of the Caribbean basin.

## The art world comes south

Nothing announced Miami’s cultural reinvention more decisively than the arrival of Art Basel Miami Beach in 2002.

The annual fair turned early December into one of the most important weeks on the global art calendar. Collectors, curators, celebrities and partygoers descend on South Florida for exhibitions, satellite fairs, installations and events stretching from Miami Beach to the mainland.

But the city’s art scene is no longer confined to one week.

The Pérez Art Museum Miami, overlooking Biscayne Bay, has become a landmark for modern and contemporary art, with a strong focus on the Americas. Nearby, the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami anchors a growing institutional presence in the Design District. Private collections and smaller galleries add depth to a scene once dismissed as little more than an art-market party.

Wynwood offers the most visible symbol of that evolution.

Formerly a warehouse district, the neighborhood became an open-air canvas for muralists and street artists. Its colorful walls helped draw visitors, galleries, restaurants and breweries. Development followed quickly — perhaps too quickly for some longtime residents and artists, who have watched rents rise and the neighborhood’s raw, improvised character become increasingly commercial.

That tension is part of contemporary Miami: creativity often arrives alongside speculation, and reinvention can come at the cost of displacement.

## Design beyond the beach

Miami’s aesthetic identity has always mattered.

South Beach’s restored Art Deco buildings remain among the city’s defining sights, their curved corners and geometric facades recalling the optimism of the 1930s. A walk along Ocean Drive or Collins Avenue reveals a city that understood branding long before the term became fashionable.

But Miami design now extends well beyond retro hotels.

In the Design District, luxury fashion houses sit beside public art, experimental architecture and high-end furniture showrooms. Even visitors with no intention of shopping can wander among installations and striking buildings that turn the neighborhood into a polished outdoor gallery.

Elsewhere, tropical modernism is enjoying renewed appreciation. Architects and designers are embracing shaded courtyards, indoor-outdoor spaces, lush landscaping and materials suited to heat and humidity.

The city’s look remains extravagant, but increasingly it is also thoughtful — shaped by climate, migration and the desire to create something distinctly Miami rather than simply importing styles from New York or Los Angeles.

## A dining scene with many accents

For years, Miami food was reduced to a handful of clichés: Cuban sandwiches, stone crab and oversized cocktails by the beach.

Those remain worth seeking out. A cafecito from a walk-up ventanita is still one of the city’s essential rituals, and a plate of croquetas can function as breakfast, snack or late-night recovery meal.

But Miami’s dining landscape is now far broader.

In Little Havana, Cuban institutions coexist with contemporary restaurants and cocktail bars. In Little Haiti, Caribbean flavors tell the story of another community central to the city’s identity. Peruvian ceviche, Venezuelan arepas, Colombian baked goods, Argentine steaks and Nikkei cuisine reflect generations of migration and cultural exchange.

A new wave of chefs has also made Miami a destination for tasting menus, seafood-driven restaurants and inventive neighborhood dining. Michelin’s arrival in Florida reinforced what local diners already knew: Miami’s food scene had matured.

Still, some of the best meals remain the least formal — eaten at a counter, purchased from a bakery or served in a strip mall far from the beachfront glamour.

Miami rewards travelers willing to leave the postcard behind.

## Nightlife grows up — without settling down

Miami has never struggled to stay awake.

The city’s nightlife reputation was built on South Beach megaclubs, celebrity DJs and all-night parties. Those experiences still exist, joined by sprawling venues where electronic music can continue well past sunrise.

But the nightlife has diversified.

Rooftop bars overlook the Brickell skyline. Intimate lounges specialize in rum, mezcal and tropical cocktails. Live Latin music fills clubs in Little Havana, while Wynwood and downtown attract crowds to breweries, dance floors and hybrid spaces that blur the line between gallery, restaurant and party.

The mood can change within a few blocks — from salsa to techno, from a hotel lobby piano to a warehouse rave.

That variety reflects the city itself: polished and chaotic, exclusive and open, always performing but rarely predictable.

## A city still being reinvented

Miami’s transformation is not without contradictions.

Luxury towers rise amid a severe affordability crisis. Neighborhoods shaped by immigrant and working-class communities face intense development pressure. And climate change poses an existential challenge to a low-lying city already familiar with flooding, extreme heat and hurricanes.

The future of Miami will depend not only on how many galleries, restaurants or hotels it can attract, but on whether the people who created its culture can afford to remain part of it.

For travelers, that means looking beyond the glossy surface.

Yes, visit the pastel hotels and palm-lined beaches. But also ride through Little Havana, explore the museums, seek out Caribbean restaurants, study the murals and listen for the rapid shifts between English, Spanish and Creole.

The speedboats and neon haven’t disappeared. Neither has the city’s appetite for spectacle.

But the Miami of today is no longer simply the backdrop to someone else’s fantasy. It is a cosmopolitan center with its own artistic language, culinary confidence and restless sense of possibility — a city that took the myth of “Miami Vice” and turned it into something richer, messier and far more interesting.

counterfactuals.output:
# Miami: From Seaside Escape to Global Cultural Capital

Miami has always been a city in motion. Built between ocean and swamp, shaped by migration and reinvention, it has repeatedly transformed crisis into spectacle and diversity into identity. What began as a subtropical resort at the edge of the United States is now an international center of art, architecture, food, and Latin American culture.

## A Resort Rises from the Mangroves

Miami’s early growth was driven by the promise of escape. After the arrival of Henry Flagler’s railroad in 1896, tourists and developers began seeing South Florida as a winter refuge—a place of warm water, palm trees, and seemingly limitless land. Across Biscayne Bay, Miami Beach emerged in the early 20th century as a purpose-built resort, with hotels, bathing clubs, and oceanfront promenades catering to visitors from colder northern states.

The real-estate boom of the 1920s turned Miami into a national sensation. Mediterranean Revival mansions, lavish hotels, and new neighborhoods appeared at extraordinary speed. Although hurricanes and financial collapse ended the boom, Miami Beach continued to develop during the 1930s and 1940s.

That era produced one of the city’s defining visual legacies: **Art Deco architecture**. Along Ocean Drive and throughout what is now the Miami Beach Architectural District, architects created streamlined hotels in pastel colors, decorated with porthole windows, geometric motifs, neon signs, and nautical flourishes. Buildings such as the Colony, Breakwater, and Carlyle projected an optimistic vision of modern life. Their preservation decades later helped turn South Beach itself into an open-air museum.

## A Gateway to the Americas

Miami’s identity changed dramatically after the Cuban Revolution of 1959. Hundreds of thousands of Cuban exiles arrived over the following decades, bringing businesses, political networks, music, cuisine, and a strong sense of cultural continuity. Little Havana became a center of Cuban American life, while Spanish increasingly joined English as one of the city’s everyday languages.

Later arrivals from Colombia, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Argentina, Brazil, and elsewhere deepened Miami’s international character. Rather than simply influencing the city, **Latin American communities became central to its economy and culture**. Miami developed into a financial, media, and commercial bridge between the United States, the Caribbean, and Latin America.

This transformation was not always smooth. Questions of race, class, language, and political power created tensions that periodically erupted into public conflict. Yet migration also gave Miami the energy and entrepreneurial ambition that would drive its later reinventions.

## The Turbulent 1980s

During the 1980s, Miami acquired a darker global reputation. The city became a major transit point in the cocaine trade, and violent competition among traffickers produced the era commonly remembered as the “Cocaine Cowboys” period. Drug money moved through banks, real estate, nightclubs, and luxury businesses, blurring the boundaries between legitimate growth and criminal wealth.

At the same time, the 1980 Mariel boatlift brought about 125,000 Cubans to South Florida in a matter of months, straining public services and intensifying political debates. Racial inequality and distrust of law enforcement contributed to unrest, including the Liberty City uprising after the acquittal of police officers in the death of Arthur McDuffie.

Popular culture turned these pressures into a seductive image. *Miami Vice* presented a city of speedboats, white suits, neon skylines, and sudden violence. The television series exaggerated Miami’s glamour and danger, but it also helped revive interest in South Beach. Its vivid aesthetic drew attention to aging Art Deco buildings that preservationists were fighting to save.

The decade’s contradictions became part of Miami’s mythology: dazzling wealth beside deep poverty, tropical leisure beside urban volatility, American ambition expressed through unmistakably Caribbean and Latin rhythms.

## Reinvention Through Culture

By the 1990s and early 2000s, Miami was remaking itself again. South Beach became an international destination for nightlife, fashion, photography, and design. Restored Art Deco hotels gave the city a recognizable architectural brand, while its multilingual population attracted global companies, media networks, and creative professionals.

A pivotal moment came in 2002 with the launch of **Art Basel Miami Beach**. The annual fair connected Miami to the international art market, drawing collectors, galleries, artists, celebrities, and satellite events from around the world. Each December, the city becomes a vast cultural stage, with installations, exhibitions, parties, and performances extending far beyond the main convention center.

Art Basel also accelerated the rise of Miami’s year-round arts institutions and private collections. Museums expanded, galleries multiplied, and neighborhoods once considered peripheral became creative centers.

No district symbolizes that shift more clearly than **Wynwood**. Formerly dominated by warehouses and light industry, the neighborhood became known for enormous murals, experimental galleries, studios, breweries, and restaurants. The Wynwood Walls outdoor museum helped establish street art as a major tourist attraction. Although the district’s popularity has brought development and concerns about gentrification, its transformation demonstrated Miami’s ability to turn overlooked urban spaces into cultural landmarks.

## A Renaissance with Latin American Roots

Modern Miami’s renaissance cannot be separated from its Latin American influence. It is heard in salsa, reggaeton, Spanish-language radio, and conversations that move fluidly between languages. It is tasted in Cuban coffee, Venezuelan arepas, Peruvian ceviche, Haitian griot, and inventive restaurants that combine Caribbean, Latin, and North American traditions. It is visible in contemporary art, fashion, festivals, and architecture.

Today, Miami is more than a beach resort, more than an Art Deco postcard, and more than the crime-haunted city of 1980s legend. It is a place where identities overlap: Southern and Caribbean, American and Latin American, historic and futuristic.

Its greatest talent may be reinvention. Miami has repeatedly absorbed new people, survived upheaval, and converted its contradictions into culture. The result is a city whose glamour is real—but whose deeper appeal lies in the restless, multicultural energy beneath the surface.

## Miami Has Changed the Channel

**MIAMI —** The first surprise comes at sunrise.

Along Biscayne Bay, runners glide past glass towers glowing peach and gold. A driverless people mover rattles above downtown streets. In Brickell, office workers queue for Cuban coffee beneath skyscrapers that did not exist when *Miami Vice* sent detectives Crockett and Tubbs speeding through the night in a white Ferrari.

The television series, broadcast from 1984 to 1989, fixed Miami in the global imagination as a pastel fever dream: speedboats, synth music, Art Deco hotels, cocaine money and sudden violence. It was stylish—and grounded in a real period when South Florida was a major hub for drug trafficking—but it was also a carefully composed crime drama, not a complete portrait of the city.

Four decades later, Miami has changed the channel.

Massive immigration from Latin America and the Caribbean has made the metropolitan area even more international. Spanish is part of everyday public life, and communities with roots in Cuba, Haiti, Venezuela, Colombia, Argentina and elsewhere have reshaped its politics, food and culture. Little Havana remains famous, but today’s Miami story also runs through Little Haiti, Doral, Hialeah and suburban neighborhoods rarely seen in the neon-lit series.

The skyline has transformed just as dramatically. Brickell, once a quieter banking district, is now a dense canyon of condominium towers, restaurants and financial offices. Downtown and Edgewater have boomed, while Miami Beach has evolved from a fading resort zone into one of the world’s best-known—and most expensive—coastal destinations. New money has arrived from Latin America, Wall Street, technology firms and luxury real estate investors.

Culture, too, has moved beyond the show’s nightclubs and beachfront glamour. Wynwood’s murals helped turn former warehouses into a major arts-and-entertainment district. Art Basel Miami Beach made December an international art-world pilgrimage. Museums, design fairs, music scenes and ambitious restaurants now compete with the sand for visitors’ attention.

Some traces of *Miami Vice* remain. The restored Art Deco façades of South Beach still glow after dark. Cigarette boats still carve white lines across the bay. Fashion remains exuberant, and the city still knows how to make an entrance.

But the modern soundtrack includes construction cranes, reggaeton, tech conferences and anxious conversations about rent and flood insurance. Crime rates are far below the worst years associated with the cocaine era, yet inequality remains stark. Luxury towers rise near neighborhoods where residents face displacement. “Sunny-day” tidal flooding, extreme heat and stronger hurricane risks have made climate change an immediate civic concern rather than a distant forecast.

That may be the biggest difference. *Miami Vice* portrayed a city living dangerously for the night. Modern Miami is a far larger, richer and more diverse metropolis trying to secure its future—while the water inches higher around it.

Visitors can still chase the old fantasy: drive Ocean Drive at dusk, admire the pastel hotels and cue up a synthesizer-heavy playlist. But step inland, order a cafecito, ride through Brickell and listen to the languages around you. The real Miami has outgrown the television frame—even if it still looks spectacular in neon.

counterfactuals.output:
## Miami: Reinvention in the Sun

Miami sells the fantasy of endless summer: pale sand, warm Atlantic water, candy-colored lifeguard towers, and palms bending above Ocean Drive. From the broad beaches of Miami Beach and family-friendly Key Biscayne to the quieter shoreline of Surfside, the coast remains the region’s defining attraction. Yet Miami is more than a beach resort. Its identity has been shaped by repeated cycles of migration, speculation, scandal, decline, and extravagant renewal.

Tourism transformed the area in the early 20th century, when rail links, real-estate promotion, and Florida’s land boom drew winter visitors south. The development of Miami Beach—and its famous concentration of Art Deco hotels in the 1920s and 1930s—gave the destination its enduring visual language. After World War II, grand oceanfront resorts and the growing popularity of air travel turned Miami into an international vacation capital, particularly for visitors from the northeastern United States, Latin America, and Europe.

That glamorous image darkened during the late 1970s and 1980s. Miami became a major gateway for cocaine smuggled from Colombia and the Caribbean, generating vast illicit wealth alongside gang violence, corruption, and sensational headlines. The “Cocaine Cowboys” era became embedded in popular culture through films, documentaries, and television series such as *Miami Vice*. Although the period’s violence has receded, its legacy remains part of the city’s mythology: a cautionary counterpoint to the sunshine-and-luxury narrative.

By the 1990s, South Beach was reinventing itself. Preservationists had already helped save the Art Deco district from demolition, and designers, photographers, models, restaurateurs, and nightlife entrepreneurs began returning to the neighborhood. Aging properties were converted into stylish boutique hotels, often preserving pastel façades while introducing minimalist interiors, rooftop pools, and scene-driven bars. This revival established a formula that still defines Miami hospitality: historic architecture repackaged with contemporary design and theatrical glamour.

Art has become another pillar of the city’s international reputation. Art Basel Miami Beach, launched in 2002, anchors a sprawling annual art week of fairs, installations, parties, and satellite events. Wynwood’s warehouses and murals helped popularize the district as a street-art destination, while institutions such as Pérez Art Museum Miami, the Institute of Contemporary Art, The Bass, and the Rubell Museum support a broader year-round scene. As development pushes artists into new neighborhoods, Miami’s creative geography continues to shift.

The city’s cultural energy comes above all from its population. Cuban exile communities profoundly reshaped Miami after 1959, making Spanish an everyday language and Little Havana a symbolic heartland. Later arrivals from Haiti, Colombia, Venezuela, Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, Brazil, and elsewhere across Latin America and the Caribbean added new cuisines, music, businesses, and political traditions. Alongside long-established Black communities, Jewish residents, retirees, and more recent domestic migrants, they have made greater Miami one of the most multicultural urban regions in the United States.

Through every reinvention, the party endures. Miami nightlife moves between South Beach clubs, downtown rooftops, Wynwood bars, Latin dance floors, waterfront lounges, pool parties, and marathon electronic-music events. The scene can be exclusive, expensive, and unapologetically performative, but it is also central to the destination’s appeal. Miami remains a place where leisure is treated as spectacle—and where the next version of the city is often being invented after dark.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nostalgic but informative CNN travel piece titled around the idea that Miami has “gone to rehab,” contrasting white Armani suits and gangland shootouts with today’s galleries, Design District, international culture, and stylish nightlife.
counterfactuals.output:
# Miami has gone to rehab — and emerged more stylish than ever

**White Armani suits, pastel hotels and gangland shootouts once defined Miami’s image. Today, the city’s galleries, global culture and sophisticated nightlife reveal a destination that has reinvented itself without erasing its flamboyant past.**

**Miami, Florida (CNN) —** There was a time when Miami arrived on television in a white Ferrari, sleeves rolled above the elbows and Phil Collins brooding on the stereo.

The city of the 1980s — or at least the version broadcast around the world — wore white Armani suits, carried too much cash and seemed perpetually one bad nightclub deal away from a gangland shootout.

That image wasn’t entirely fictional. Cocaine money, violent crime and political turbulence marked the era, while “Miami Vice” turned the city’s danger, Art Deco architecture and tropical light into a seductive global brand.

Four decades later, Miami has gone to rehab.

It hasn’t become quieter, exactly. Nor has it surrendered its appetite for spectacle. But the city once caricatured as America’s sunburned frontier has matured into an international capital of art, design, food and nightlife.

The white suits are now more likely to appear at a gallery opening. The old warehouses host installations rather than illicit cargo. And the soundtrack, once dominated by synth-pop, has expanded to include Cuban son, Haitian compas, Argentine electronic music, Brazilian funk and the bass-heavy pulse of clubs that don’t fill up until well after midnight.

## Pastels, preservation and reinvention

Miami’s rehabilitation begins on South Beach, where the streamlined hotels of the Art Deco Historic District still glow in shades of mint, peach and flamingo pink.

In the 1970s, many of these buildings were deteriorating and threatened with demolition. Preservationists, led by activist Barbara Baer Capitman, helped save the neighborhood’s architectural character. By the 1980s and ’90s, fashion photographers, models and celebrities had rediscovered Ocean Drive.

Today, the district remains Miami’s most recognizable façade. Early mornings are the best time to appreciate it: before the convertibles begin circling, before restaurant hosts start waving oversized menus and before the beach becomes a catwalk.

A stroll along Ocean Drive and Collins Avenue reveals the details often lost behind the neon — terrazzo floors, nautical windows, chrome railings and geometric “eyebrows” designed to block the fierce Florida sun.

South Beach can still be theatrical and expensive, but several blocks inland the mood changes. Cafés, neighborhood restaurants and low-rise residential streets offer a quieter version of Miami Beach, one less interested in being photographed.

## The Design District grows up

Across Biscayne Bay, the Miami Design District presents the city’s transformation in its most polished form.

Once known primarily for furniture showrooms and neglected warehouses, the neighborhood has become a compact showcase of contemporary architecture, public art, luxury retail and ambitious dining.

Buildings by internationally known architects sit beside installations that reward wandering. The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami offers a serious cultural counterpoint to the designer storefronts, while nearby galleries and studios connect the district to the broader local art scene.

The area can feel immaculate — Miami with its shirt tucked in — but its evolution reflects a larger shift. Design is no longer decorative here; it has become one of the city’s industries and identities.

The annual arrival of Art Basel Miami Beach helped accelerate that change. Every December, collectors, artists, celebrities and people dressed like all three descend on the city. Satellite fairs, pop-up exhibitions and parties spread from Miami Beach to the mainland, briefly turning traffic into performance art.

Yet Miami’s gallery culture exists beyond that one feverish week. The city’s museums, private collections and independent spaces now make it possible to plan an art-focused visit at almost any time of year.

## Beyond the Wynwood walls

Just south of the Design District, Wynwood became famous for transforming warehouse walls into monumental canvases.

The neighborhood’s murals helped establish Miami as a center for street art and made Wynwood Walls one of the city’s most visited attractions. It also brought a familiar cycle: artists arrived, then restaurants and breweries, followed by developers, apartments and rising rents.

Some of Wynwood’s rawness has been polished away, but it remains a useful introduction to Miami’s creative energy. The best approach is to look beyond the central attraction. Smaller galleries, shops and side-street murals reveal a district still negotiating what happens when an underground scene becomes a tourism brand.

For a more institutional view of contemporary culture, the waterfront Pérez Art Museum Miami combines international exhibitions with one of the city’s most inviting public spaces. Its shaded terraces overlook Biscayne Bay, offering a reminder that in Miami even serious art competes with the weather.

Next door, the Phillip and Patricia Frost Museum of Science adds aquariums, a planetarium and family-friendly relief from the afternoon heat.

## A city assembled from elsewhere

Miami is often described as a gateway to Latin America. Spend a day here and the phrase begins to feel inadequate. The city is not merely a gateway; it is a crossroads, a headquarters and, for generations of arrivals, a second chance.

Cuban influence remains foundational. In Little Havana, dominoes clack beneath the trees at Máximo Gómez Park, cafecito is served in quantities small enough to seem harmless, and conversations along Calle Ocho move easily between family news, baseball and politics.

But Miami’s identity stretches far beyond a single diaspora.

Haitian culture animates Little Haiti through food, music, art and community institutions. Venezuelan arepas, Colombian bakeries, Nicaraguan fritangas and Peruvian ceviche are embedded in the city’s daily life. Spanish is often the default language, though English, Haitian Creole, Portuguese and French are never far away.

This international character is most vivid at the table. Miami dining once leaned heavily on hotel restaurants, steakhouses and the idea that every plate required a tropical garnish. The modern city is more confident.

Chefs draw on Caribbean ingredients, Latin American traditions and Florida seafood without treating them as novelties. Excellent meals can be found in glamorous dining rooms, suburban strip malls and walk-up windows where a strong coffee costs less than parking at the beach.

## Nightlife trades vice for velvet ropes

Miami’s nocturnal reputation has also evolved, though moderation remains a relative concept.

The city still offers enormous clubs, celebrity DJs and bottle-service rituals conducted with sparklers. South Beach remains a reliable stage for late-night excess, while downtown and Brickell cater to a sharply dressed crowd moving between rooftop bars, restaurants and lounges.

But stylish nightlife no longer means only standing behind a velvet rope.

Listening bars, cocktail lounges, live-music venues and hotel terraces offer alternatives to the mega-club. In Little Havana, salsa spills onto sidewalks. In Wynwood, breweries and dance floors share blocks with galleries. Along the Miami River, restaurants turn into waterside parties as yachts glide past the tables.

The unifying principle is lateness. Dinner at 10 p.m. is not unusual. A club that looks empty at midnight may simply not have started.

Miami nights still reward confidence — and comfortable shoes.

## What the old Miami left behind

For all its reinvention, Miami hasn’t severed ties with its former selves.

The Art Deco hotels remain. Speedboats still carve across the bay. A white linen suit, worn without irony, is never entirely out of place. The city continues to flirt with danger, glamour and reinvention because those qualities are not just television mythology; they are part of its civic personality.

But the old clichés now share space with something more layered.

Miami is a city where collectors discuss conceptual art over Cuban coffee, where a former warehouse can become a Michelin-starred restaurant, and where a night out may begin with an exhibition and end with dancing beneath palm trees.

It has gone to rehab, but it hasn’t lost its vice.

It has simply learned to curate it.

---

## If you go

**Best time to visit:**  
November through April brings lower humidity and generally pleasant temperatures, along with higher hotel prices. Summer is hot, wet and hurricane-prone, but often more affordable.

**Getting around:**  
A car is useful for exploring widely, though traffic and parking can be frustrating. Rideshares are plentiful. Metromover is free and convenient for parts of downtown and Brickell.

**Don’t miss:**  
- The Art Deco Historic District at sunrise  
- The Miami Design District and ICA Miami  
- Wynwood’s murals and galleries  
- Pérez Art Museum Miami  
- Little Havana, especially around Calle Ocho  
- A waterfront drink at sunset  
- At least one late-night cafecito

**Local rhythm:**  
Plan less than you think you can accomplish. Neighborhoods are spread out, traffic is unpredictable and Miami tends to reveal itself between scheduled stops.
